brief.situation: You are the cloud security analyst at Fernhill Analytics, a fictional data company. At 14:05 two alerts land together: the code host's secret scanning found the build pipeline's access key in a public repository, and the cloud audit trail shows that key creating a new administrator user. Work the incident: investigate, contain, preserve evidence, and report.
handover: The pipeline user ci-deploy uses a long-lived access key. The customer-exports bucket holds customer data. The audit trail covers every Region and is kept for a year.
The account has a write-once case bucket for evidence.
howItWorks: Each task takes analyst time: choose it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes that task takes. The attacker keeps working on the same clock.
New alerts and log lines appear in the console as they happen.
When you declare the incident contained, you notify, write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident record: how the attacker got in and stayed in, why you contained each identity the way you did, and what you kept as evidence.

parts.label: Access and persistence
parts.criteria: Names the leaked long-lived key in a public repository as initial access, and the administrator user (and any role trusting an outside account) as persistence the attacker made with it.
parts.modelAnswer: A long-lived access key for the pipeline was committed to a public repository; from 13:51 someone else used it to create support-ops with administrator rights and its own key, which is persistence that survives deactivating the leaked key.

parts.label: Containment
parts.criteria: Deactivates (does not delete) the leaked key and quarantines every attacker-made identity with a deny-all policy; explains why an IP block alone does not contain it (the attacker changes address); checks every Region for resources.
parts.modelAnswer: I deactivated ci-deploy's key without deleting it, then deactivated support-ops's key with a deny-all policy, after reviewing every identity made in the last day. Blocking the address would not help: the credentials work from any address.

parts.label: Evidence and eradication
parts.criteria: Copies the audit trail and IAM records to write-once storage and snapshots instances before terminating them; then deletes the attacker's identities and replaces the long-lived key with short-lived role credentials.
parts.modelAnswer: Before deleting or terminating anything I copied the audit trail and the identities' records to the write-once case bucket, and snapshotted any instance; then I deleted the attacker's identities and moved the pipeline to a short-lived role.

expertPath.text: Read the audit trail for the leaked key: it created an administrator. Deactivate the key (keep it) and quarantine support-ops.

contained.headline: Good: contained before the data moved
contained.body: You cut the leaked key and the attacker's administrator before either could build more, checked for anything else they made, and kept the trail first.

containedLate.headline: Contained, with gaps
containedLate.body: The attacker is out. The criteria show what cost you: a later containment, a second backdoor, or copying that had started.

exfil.headline: Customer data copied out
exfil.body: Deactivating only the leaked key, or blocking one address, left the attacker's own administrator working. Shut every identity the key created.

evidenceLost.headline: Evidence destroyed
evidenceLost.body: Terminating the instances before a snapshot removes the only record of what ran on them. Back up, then terminate.

stillIn.headline: Closed too soon
stillIn.body: A working key, user or role is a way back in. Account for every means of persistent access before eradication (CISA).

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: A long-lived key leaked in a public repository and used from a new address to create an administrator is a compromise with persistence. Deactivate the key (keep it), quarantine every identity it created after listing them, escalate, keep the audit trail, the identities' records and any instance snapshots in write-once storage before terminating or deleting, then delete the attacker's identities and move the pipeline to short-lived role credentials, and notify the incident lead, leadership, legal and privacy.
